summary: Arabic is a Semitic language. This course teaches Modern Standard Arabic, the shared written and formal language of the Arab world; everyday speech is in regional dialects. It is written from right to left, and words are built from consonant roots.

typology.why: Words are built by weaving a consonant root into a vowel pattern (k-t-b: كَتَبَ kataba ‘he wrote’, كِتَاب kitāb ‘book’), and one ending carries person, number and gender at once.
typology.alsoShows: Small words are attached in front or behind like pieces: وَ wa- ‘and’, الْ al- ‘the’, possessive endings.

facts.label: Script
facts.value: Arabic script, right to left; letters join and change shape; short vowels are usually not written

facts.label: Where
facts.value: official language of more than 20 countries from Morocco to Iraq; the language of the Qur’an

peculiarities.title: Roots and patterns
peculiarities.text: Most words share a root of three consonants with their relatives; the vowels and extra letters around it give the meaning.

peculiarities.title: No ‘to be’ in the present
peculiarities.text: أَنَا طَالِبٌ ʾana ṭālibun = ‘I (am) a student’: the present tense of ‘to be’ is not said.

peculiarities.title: Unwritten vowels
peculiarities.text: Short vowels are marks above and below the letters; normal texts leave them out. This course shows them until you can read without them.

peculiarities.title: Gender everywhere
peculiarities.text: Two genders, and ‘you’, verbs and adjectives change with them: أَنْتَ anta (to a man), أَنْتِ anti (to a woman).

forYou.text: Many Turkish words come from Arabic — kitap (كِتَاب), merhaba (مَرْحَبًا), kalem (قَلَم): use them as bridges.
Gender and agreement work as in Greek, but there are only two genders and a dual for pairs.

quiz.why: Roots woven into patterns, and endings that carry several meanings at once.

quiz.q: How do you say ‘I am a student’?
options: with the verb كَانَ in the present
quiz.why: The present of ‘to be’ is not said.

quiz.q: What do كِتَاب, كَاتِب and كَتَبَ have in common?
quiz.why: All three are built on the root of ‘writing’.
